content: 1. Transmission of infectious agents through mucosal surfaces of the eyes, mouth, nasal passages, throat, or pharynx of another person primarily occurs via large respiratory droplets. These droplets, which constitute more than 99% of the volume, travel short distances (less than 1 meter) and do not remain suspended in the air. Therefore, specialized air handling and ventilation systems are not required to prevent droplet transmission. 2. Ebola disease (EBOD), previously referred to as Ebola hemorrhagic fever, is a severe and often fatal illness that affects humans and other primates. It is caused by various species of the Ebola virus. Transmission can occur through direct contact with bodily fluids or contaminated objects, such as bedding or clothing. 3. A fomite is any object, such as a dish, doorknob, or article of clothing, that may become contaminated with infectious agents like bacteria or viruses and facilitate their transmission. 4. A health worker is defined as anyone primarily engaged in activities aimed at improving health. The term health and care worker is used to encompass both health workers and care workers. 5. Hygiene kits are distributed to families and individuals identified as part of an Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) ring, such as churches, schools, or communities, to prevent the transmission of the Ebola virus. These kits typically include items like hand soap, laundry soap, and educational materials to raise awareness. 6. Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) is a practical, evidence-based approach designed to protect patients, health workers, and care workers from avoidable infections. It involves implementing measures to prevent harm caused by infectious agents. 7. Marburg disease (MARD) is a highly virulent illness that causes hemorrhagic fever and has a case fatality rate of up to 88%. It is caused by the Marburg virus, which belongs to the same family as the Ebola virus. Human infection with the Marburg virus often results from prolonged exposure to mines or caves inhabited by Rousettus bat colonies. 8. The no-touch technique is a method used by health and care workers during screening activities. It involves maintaining a distance of at least 1 meter from the individuals being screened and avoiding physical contact by utilizing engineering controls. 9. Personal protective equipment (PPE) refers to specialized equipment designed to prevent or minimize exposure to hazards, including biological, chemical, radiological, electrical, or mechanical risks. PPE is essential for protecting health and care workers from radiological and biological hazards. 10. Reprocessing involves all necessary steps to prepare a contaminated, reusable medical device for reuse. This process includes cleaning, functional testing, packaging, labeling, disinfection, and sterilization. 11. Screening is the process of evaluating an individual to determine whether they meet a standardized case definition for a specific condition or disease. 12. Standard precautions are measures aimed at protecting both health workers and patients by reducing the risk of microorganism transmission from recognized and unrecognized sources. These precautions represent the minimum standard of IPC practices and should be consistently applied in all healthcare settings during patient care. 13. Spraying refers to the application of a liquid in the form of a fine mist onto a surface, item, or device using an atomizer or sprayer. 14. Transmission-based precautions (TBP) are additional measures implemented alongside standard precautions for patients with known or suspected infections caused by transmissible or epidemiologically significant pathogens. The type of TBP depends on the microorganism's transmission route, such as contact, droplet, or airborne. 15. Triage is the process of categorizing patients based on the urgency of their need for medical intervention. It identifies those requiring immediate care and those who can safely wait. Triage typically involves close physical contact (within 1 meter) with the patient during assessment. 16. Wiping involves cleaning or drying a surface by rubbing it with a cloth or paper towel. In healthcare facilities, surfaces are systematically wiped with cloths soaked in water or detergent, rinsed, and then wiped again with an approved disinfectant. 17. Zoonotic transmission refers to the natural transmission of diseases or infections from vertebrate animals to humans.
